1.o: In the close of the foregoing book we read how God magnified Solomon and Israel obeyed him; God and Israel concurred to honour him. Now here we have an account, I. How he honoured God by sacrifice (ver. 1-6) and by prayer, ver. 7-12. II. How he honoured Israel by increasing their strength, wealth, and trade, ver. 13-17.
1.s: Solomon Asks for Wisdom at Gibeon
1.i: Second Chronicles 1 and 2 begin Solomon's reign with the most famous request in the Bible, and then with the first practical steps toward the temple.
1.p: Lord, give us wisdom to serve those You have put in our care, and teach us to build only what honors You. Amen.
1.l: If God asked what you wanted most, what would you say? Tell God today what is really in your heart.
q: Two people may serve God in different ways and neither should be censured. Whose way of serving have you judged?

2.o: Solomon's trading, which we read of in the close of the foregoing chapter, and the encouragement he gave both to merchandise and manufacturers, were very commendable. But building was the work he was designed for, and to that business he is here applying himself. Here is, I. Solomon's determination to build the temple and a royal palace, and his appointing labourers to be employed herein, ver. 1, 2, 17, 18. II. His request to Huram king of Tyre to furnish him both with artists and materials, ver. 3-10. III.
2.s: Solomon Asks for Wisdom at Gibeon
2.i: Second Chronicles 1 and 2 begin Solomon's reign with the most famous request in the Bible, and then with the first practical steps toward the temple.
2.p: Lord, give us wisdom to serve those You have put in our care, and teach us to build only what honors You. Amen.
2.l: If God asked what you wanted most, what would you say? Tell God today what is really in your heart.
q: Two people may serve God in different ways and neither should be censured. Whose way of serving have you judged?

3.o: It was a much larger and more particular account of the building of the temple which we had in the book of Kings than is here in this book of Chronicles. In this chapter we have, I. The place and time of building the temple, ver. 1, 2. II. The dimensions and rich ornaments of it, ver. 3-9. III. The cherubim in the most holy place, ver. 10-13. IV. The veil, ver. 14. V. The two pillars, ver. 15-17. Of all this we have already and an account, 1 Kings vi., vii.
3.i: Second Chronicles 3 and 4 give the temple's size and furnishings, and begin by naming the hill.
3.p: Lord, You made a place where Your people could meet You. Thank You for the places in our lives where You have met us. Amen.
3.l: Build something carefully today, even something small, as a gift to God.
q: The temple was built where the Lord had already appeared to David. What place in your life is already holy because God met you there?

4.o: We have here a further account of the furniture of God's house. I. Those things that were of brass. The altar for burnt-offerings (ver. 1), the sea and lavers to hold water (ver. 2-6), the plates with which the doors of the court were overlaid (ver. 9), the vessels of the altar, and other things, ver. 10-18. II. Those that were of gold. The candlesticks and tables (ver. 7, 8), the altar of incense (ver. 19), and the appurtenances of each of these, ver. 20-22. All these, except the brazen altar (ver.
4.i: Second Chronicles 3 and 4 give the temple's size and furnishings, and begin by naming the hill.
4.p: Lord, You made a place where Your people could meet You. Thank You for the places in our lives where You have met us. Amen.
4.l: Build something carefully today, even something small, as a gift to God.
q: The temple was built where the Lord had already appeared to David. What place in your life is already holy because God met you there?

5.o: The temple being built and furnished for God, we have here, I. Possession given to him, by bringing in the dedicated things (ver. 1), but especially the ark, the token of his presence, ver. 2-10. II. Possession taken by him, in a cloud, ver. 11-14. For if any man open the door of his heart to God he will come in, Rev. iii. 20.
5.i: Second Chronicles 5 to 7 record the dedication of the temple, in which the glory of God came down and filled the house.
5.p: Lord, You are good, and Your love endures forever. Fill our homes and churches with Your presence, and hear us when we pray. Amen.
5.l: Pray today with your whole heart for your town or your country, and ask God to heal it.
q: What did you give lately that you never heard anything back about, and does that matter?

6.o: The glory of the Lord, in the vehicle of a thick cloud, having filled the house which Solomon built, by which God manifested his presence there, he immediately improves the opportunity, and addresses God, as a God now, in a peculiar manner, nigh at hand. I. He makes a solemn declaration of his intention in building this house, to the satisfaction of the people and the honour of God, both of whom he blessed, ver. 1-11. II.
6.i: Second Chronicles 5 to 7 record the dedication of the temple, in which the glory of God came down and filled the house.
6.p: Lord, You are good, and Your love endures forever. Fill our homes and churches with Your presence, and hear us when we pray. Amen.
6.l: Pray today with your whole heart for your town or your country, and ask God to heal it.
q: What did you give lately that you never heard anything back about, and does that matter?

7.o: In this chapter we have God's answer to Solomon's prayer. I. His public answer by fire from heaven, which consumed the sacrifices (ver. 1), with which the priests and people were much affected, ver. 2, 3. By that token of God's acceptance they were encouraged to continue the solemnities of the feast for fourteen days, and Solomon was encouraged to pursue all his designs for the honour of God, ver. 4-11. II. His private answer by word of mouth, in a dream or vision of the night, ver. 12-22.
7.i: Second Chronicles 5 to 7 record the dedication of the temple, in which the glory of God came down and filled the house.
7.p: Lord, You are good, and Your love endures forever. Fill our homes and churches with Your presence, and hear us when we pray. Amen.
7.l: Pray today with your whole heart for your town or your country, and ask God to heal it.
q: What did you give lately that you never heard anything back about, and does that matter?

8.o: In this chapter we are told, I. What cities Solomon built, ver. 1-6. II. What workmen Solomon employed, ver. 7-10. III. What care he took about a proper settlement for his wife, ver. 11. IV. What a good method he put the temple-service into, ver. 12-16. V. What trading he had with foreign countries, ver. 17, 18.
8.i: The queen of Sheba crossed Arabia to see whether the stories about Solomon were true, and found that not half had been told.
8.p: Lord, You give wisdom to all who ask. Make us teachable, and let us put You first in everything we build. Amen.
8.l: Ask someone wise in your family one hard question this week, and listen all the way to the end of the answer.
q: Solomon's success came from building God's house first, and quickly. What do you put first, and does it show in the rest of your work?

9.o: Solomon here continues to appear great both at home and abroad. We had this account of his grandeur, 1 Kings x. Nothing is here added; but his defection towards his latter end, which we have there (ch. xi.), is here omitted, and the close of this chapter brings him to the grave with an unstained reputation. Perhaps none of the chapters in the Chronicles agree so much with a chapter in the Kings as this does with 1 Kings x.
9.i: The queen of Sheba crossed Arabia to see whether the stories about Solomon were true, and found that not half had been told.
9.p: Lord, You give wisdom to all who ask. Make us teachable, and let us put You first in everything we build. Amen.
9.l: Ask someone wise in your family one hard question this week, and listen all the way to the end of the answer.
q: Solomon's success came from building God's house first, and quickly. What do you put first, and does it show in the rest of your work?

10.o: This chapter is copied almost verbatim from 1 Kings xii. 1-19, where it was opened at large. Solomon's defection from God was not repeated, but the defection of the ten tribes from his family is, in this chapter, where we find, I. How foolish Rehoboam was in his treating with them, ver. 1, 5-14. II. How wicked the people were in complaining of Solomon (ver. 2-4) and forsaking Rehoboam, ver. 16-19. III. How just and righteous God was in all this, ver. 15. His counsel was thereby fulfilled.
10.i: Second Chronicles 10 to 12 tell how one harsh reply split Israel, and how Rehoboam's strength turned into pride.
10.p: Lord, give us humble hearts and wise advisers. Keep us from pride when we are strong, and bring us back when we stray. Amen.
10.l: Listen today to the wisest person you know before you answer a hard question.
q: They had plenty and still complained. What do you have enough of that you still call a burden?

11.o: We are here going on with the history of Rehoboam. I. His attempt to recover the ten tribes he has lost, and the letting fall of that attempt in obedience to the divine command, ver. 1-4. II. His successful endeavours to preserve the two tribes that remained, ver. 5-12. III. The resort of the priests and Levites to him, ver. 13-17. IV. An account of his wives and children, ver. 18-23.
11.i: Second Chronicles 10 to 12 tell how one harsh reply split Israel, and how Rehoboam's strength turned into pride.
11.p: Lord, give us humble hearts and wise advisers. Keep us from pride when we are strong, and bring us back when we stray. Amen.
11.l: Listen today to the wisest person you know before you answer a hard question.
q: They had plenty and still complained. What do you have enough of that you still call a burden?

12.o: This chapter gives us a more full account of the reign of Rehoboam than we had before in Kings and it is a very melancholy account. Methinks we are in the book of Judges again; for, I. Rehoboam and his people did evil in the sight of the Lord, ver. 1. II. God thereupon sold them into the hands of Shishak, king of Egypt, who greatly oppressed them, ver. 2-4. III. God sent a prophet to them, to expound to them the judgment and to call them to repentance, ver. 5. IV. They thereupon humbled themselves, ver. 6. V.
12.i: Second Chronicles 10 to 12 tell how one harsh reply split Israel, and how Rehoboam's strength turned into pride.
12.p: Lord, give us humble hearts and wise advisers. Keep us from pride when we are strong, and bring us back when we stray. Amen.
12.l: Listen today to the wisest person you know before you answer a hard question.
q: They had plenty and still complained. What do you have enough of that you still call a burden?

13.o: We have here a much fuller account of the reign of Abijah, the son of Rehoboam, than we had in the Kings. There we found that his character was no better than his father's—he "walked in the sins of his father, and his heart was not right with God," 1 Kings xv. 2, 3. But here we find him more brave and successful in war than his father was. He reigned but three years, and was chiefly famous for a glorious victory he obtained over the forces of Jeroboam. Here we have, I.
13.i: Second Chronicles 13 to 16 follow two kings, Abijah and Asa, and show that trusting God works in war but must keep working in peace.
13.p: Lord, You support those whose hearts are fully Yours. Keep us trusting You in big and small things, in war and in peace. Amen.
13.l: Pray about a small problem today, not just the big ones, and trust God with both.
q: The same war can be right in one hand and wrong in another. What makes the difference between defense and aggression in your own arguments?

14.o: In this and the two following chapters we have the history of the reign of Asa, a good reign and a long one. In this chapter we have, I. His piety, ver. 1-5. II. His policy, ver. 6-8. III. His prosperity, and particularly a glorious victory he obtained over a great army of Ethiopians that came out against him, ver. 9-15.
14.i: Second Chronicles 13 to 16 follow two kings, Abijah and Asa, and show that trusting God works in war but must keep working in peace.
14.p: Lord, You support those whose hearts are fully Yours. Keep us trusting You in big and small things, in war and in peace. Amen.
14.l: Pray about a small problem today, not just the big ones, and trust God with both.
q: The same war can be right in one hand and wrong in another. What makes the difference between defense and aggression in your own arguments?

15.o: Asa and his army were now returning in triumph from the battle, laden with spoils and adorned with the trophies of victory, the pious prince, we may now suppose, studying what he should render to God for this great favour. He knew that the work of reformation, which he had begun in his kingdom, was not perfected; his enemies abroad were subdued, but there were more dangerous enemies at home that were yet unconquered—idols in Judah and Benjamin: his victory over the former emboldened him vigorously to renew his…
15.i: Second Chronicles 13 to 16 follow two kings, Abijah and Asa, and show that trusting God works in war but must keep working in peace.
15.p: Lord, You support those whose hearts are fully Yours. Keep us trusting You in big and small things, in war and in peace. Amen.
15.l: Pray about a small problem today, not just the big ones, and trust God with both.
q: The same war can be right in one hand and wrong in another. What makes the difference between defense and aggression in your own arguments?

16.o: This chapter concludes the history of the reign of Asa, but does not furnish so pleasing an account of his latter end as we had of his beginning. I. Here is a foolish treaty with Benhadad king of Syria, ver. 1-6. II. The reproof which God sent him for it by a prophet, ver. 7-9. III. Asa's displeasure against the prophet for his faithfulness, ver. 10. IV. The sickness, death, and burial of Asa, ver. 11-14.
16.i: Second Chronicles 13 to 16 follow two kings, Abijah and Asa, and show that trusting God works in war but must keep working in peace.
16.p: Lord, You support those whose hearts are fully Yours. Keep us trusting You in big and small things, in war and in peace. Amen.
16.l: Pray about a small problem today, not just the big ones, and trust God with both.
q: The same war can be right in one hand and wrong in another. What makes the difference between defense and aggression in your own arguments?

17.o: Here begin the life and reign of Jehoshaphat, who was one of the first three among the royal worthies, one of the best that ever swayed the sceptre of Judah since David's head was laid. He was the good son of a good father, so that, as this time, grace ran in the blood, even in the blood-royal. Happy the son that had such a father, to lay a good foundation in him and for him. Happy the father that had such a son, to build so wall upon the foundation he had laid!
17.i: Second Chronicles 17 to 19 show a king who sent teachers into every town, made one big mistake, and reformed the courts.
17.p: Lord, You send teachers to every town. Give us justice in our courts and truth in our schools, and keep us from bad alliances. Amen.
17.l: Share something you have learned from the Bible with someone today, as the teachers did.
q: Ahab was more dangerous as a friend than as an enemy. Which friendship in your life asks more than it gives?

18.o: The story of this chapter we had just as it is here related in the story of the reign of Ahab king of Israel, 1 Kings xxii. There it looks more creditable to Ahab than any thing else recorded of him that he was in league with so good a man as Jehoshaphat; here it is a great blemish in the reign of Jehoshaphat that he thus connected himself with so bad a man as Ahab. Here is, I. The alliance he contracted himself with Ahab, ver. 1. II.
18.i: Second Chronicles 17 to 19 show a king who sent teachers into every town, made one big mistake, and reformed the courts.
18.p: Lord, You send teachers to every town. Give us justice in our courts and truth in our schools, and keep us from bad alliances. Amen.
18.l: Share something you have learned from the Bible with someone today, as the teachers did.
q: Ahab was more dangerous as a friend than as an enemy. Which friendship in your life asks more than it gives?

19.o: We have here a further account of the good reign of Jehoshaphat, I. His return in peace to Jerusalem, ver. 1. II. The reproof given him for his league with Ahab, and his acting in conjunction with him, ver. 2, 3. III. The great care he took thereupon to reform his kingdom, ver. 4. IV. The instructions he gave to his judges, both those in the country towns that kept the inferior courts (ver. 5-7), and those in Jerusalem that sat in the supreme judicature of the kingdom, ver. 8-11.
19.i: Second Chronicles 17 to 19 show a king who sent teachers into every town, made one big mistake, and reformed the courts.
19.p: Lord, You send teachers to every town. Give us justice in our courts and truth in our schools, and keep us from bad alliances. Amen.
19.l: Share something you have learned from the Bible with someone today, as the teachers did.
q: Ahab was more dangerous as a friend than as an enemy. Which friendship in your life asks more than it gives?

20.o: We have here, I. The great danger and distress that Jehoshaphat and his kingdom were in from a foreign invasion, ver. 1, 2. II. The pious course he took for their safety, by fasting, and praying, and seeking God, ver. 3-13. III. The assurance which God, by a prophet, immediately gave them of victory, ver. 14-17. IV. Their thankful believing reception of those assurances, ver. 18-21. V. The defeat which God gave to their enemies thereupon, ver. 22-25. VI.
20.s: The Singers Go Out Before the Army
20.i: Second Chronicles 20 is the story of a battle won by prayer, a prophecy, and a choir at the front of the army.
20.p: Lord, the battle is Yours. When we are afraid, teach us to sing, and to keep our eyes on You. Amen.
20.l: When you are afraid today, say, We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on You.
q: Fasting for sin means resolving to fast from it. What is one thing you could say no to in order to say yes to God?

21.o: Never surely did any kingdom change its king so much for the worse as Judah did, when Jehoram, one of the vilest, succeeded Jehoshaphat, one of the best. Thus were they punished for not making a better use of Jehoshaphat's good government, and their disaffectedness (or coldness at least) to his reformation, ch. xx. 33. Those that knew not now to value a good king are justly plagued with a bad one. Here is, I. Jehoram's elevation to the throne, ver. 1-3. II.
21.i: Second Chronicles 21 to 24 tell how Joash rebuilt the temple with a donation box, and how his faith died with the priest who raised him.
21.p: Lord, thank You for those who lead us well. Make our faith our own, so it does not die when they are gone. Amen.
21.l: Give something to a good cause today, and then check that you are still following what is right when no one is watching.
q: Those who mean ill are apt to suspect ill. When has your own suspicion come from something you were planning yourself?

22.o: We read, in the foregoing chapter, of the carrying away of Jehoram's sons and his wives; but here we find one of his sons and one of his wives left, his son Ahaziah and his wife Athaliah, both reserved to be the shame and plague of his family. I. Ahaziah was the shame of it as a partaker, 1. In the sin, and, 2. In the destruction, of the house of Ahab, ver. 1-9. II. Athaliah was the plague of it, for she destroyed all the seed-royal, and usurped the throne, ver. 10-12.
22.i: Second Chronicles 21 to 24 tell how Joash rebuilt the temple with a donation box, and how his faith died with the priest who raised him.
22.p: Lord, thank You for those who lead us well. Make our faith our own, so it does not die when they are gone. Amen.
22.l: Give something to a good cause today, and then check that you are still following what is right when no one is watching.
q: Those who mean ill are apt to suspect ill. When has your own suspicion come from something you were planning yourself?

23.o: Six years bloody Athaliah had tyrannised; in this chapter we have her deposed and slain, and Joash, the rightful heir, enthroned. We had the story before nearly as it is here related, 2 Kings xi. 4, &c. I. Jehoiada prepared the people for the king, acquainted them with his design, armed them, and appointed them their posts, ver. 1-10. II. He produced the king to the people, crowned him, and anointed him, ver. 11. III. He slew the usurper, ver. 12-15. IV.
23.i: Second Chronicles 21 to 24 tell how Joash rebuilt the temple with a donation box, and how his faith died with the priest who raised him.
23.p: Lord, thank You for those who lead us well. Make our faith our own, so it does not die when they are gone. Amen.
23.l: Give something to a good cause today, and then check that you are still following what is right when no one is watching.
q: Those who mean ill are apt to suspect ill. When has your own suspicion come from something you were planning yourself?

24.o: We have here the history of the reign of Joash, the progress of which, and especially its termination, were not of a piece with its beginning, nor shone with so much lustre. How wonderfully he was preserved for the throne, and placed in it, we read before; now here we are told how he began in the spirit, but ended in the flesh. I. In the beginning of his time, while Jehoiada lived, he did well; particularly, he took care to put the temple in good repair, ver. 1-14. II.
24.i: Second Chronicles 21 to 24 tell how Joash rebuilt the temple with a donation box, and how his faith died with the priest who raised him.
24.p: Lord, thank You for those who lead us well. Make our faith our own, so it does not die when they are gone. Amen.
24.l: Give something to a good cause today, and then check that you are still following what is right when no one is watching.
q: Those who mean ill are apt to suspect ill. When has your own suspicion come from something you were planning yourself?

25.o: Amaziah's reign, recorded in this chapter, was not one of the worse and yet for from good. Most of the passages in this chapter we had before more briefly related, 2 Kings xiv. Here we find Amaziah, I. A just revenger of his father's death, ver. 1-4. II. An obedient observer of the command of God, ver. 5-10. III. A cruel conqueror of the Edomites, ver. 11-13. IV. A foolish worshipper of the gods of Edom and impatient of reproof for it, ver. 14-16. V.
25.i: Second Chronicles 25 to 27 trace three kings, a wasteful mercenary deal, a king whose strength ruined him, and a king who simply walked steadily.
25.p: Lord, You help us until we are strong, and You humble the proud. Keep us from presumption, and make us steady like Jotham. Amen.
25.l: Notice today something you are proud of, and thank God for it instead of taking the credit.
q: Amaziah renamed the cliff 'subdued by God.' What would you rename the hard places in your life you have come through?

26.o: This chapter gives us an account of the reign of Uzziah (Azariah he was called in the Kings) more fully than we had it before, though it was long, and in some respects illustrious, yet it was very briefly related, 2 Kings xiv. 21; xv. 1, &c. Here is, I. His good character in general, ver. 1-5. II. His great prosperity in his wars, his buildings, and all the affairs of his kingdom, ver. 6-15. III. His presumption in invading the priests' office, for which he was struck with a leprosy, and confined by it (ver.
26.i: Second Chronicles 25 to 27 trace three kings, a wasteful mercenary deal, a king whose strength ruined him, and a king who simply walked steadily.
26.p: Lord, You help us until we are strong, and You humble the proud. Keep us from presumption, and make us steady like Jotham. Amen.
26.l: Notice today something you are proud of, and thank God for it instead of taking the credit.
q: Amaziah renamed the cliff 'subdued by God.' What would you rename the hard places in your life you have come through?

27.o: Here is a very short account of the reign of Jotham, a pious prosperous prince, of whom one would wish to have known more: but we may better dispense with the brevity of his story because that which lengthened the history of the last three kings was their degeneracy in their latter end, of which we have had a faithful account; but there was no occasion for such a melancholy conclusion of the history of this reign, which is only an account, I. Of the date and continuance of this reign, ver. 1, 8. II.
27.i: Second Chronicles 25 to 27 trace three kings, a wasteful mercenary deal, a king whose strength ruined him, and a king who simply walked steadily.
27.p: Lord, You help us until we are strong, and You humble the proud. Keep us from presumption, and make us steady like Jotham. Amen.
27.l: Notice today something you are proud of, and thank God for it instead of taking the credit.
q: Amaziah renamed the cliff 'subdued by God.' What would you rename the hard places in your life you have come through?

28.o: This chapter is the history of the reign of Ahaz the son of Jotham; a bad reign it was, and which helped to augment the fierce anger of the Lord. We have here, I. His great wickedness, ver. 1-4. II. The trouble he brought himself into by it, ver. 5-8. III. The reproof which God sent by a prophet to the army of Israel for trampling upon their brethren of Judah, and the obedient ear they gave to that reproof, ver. 9-15. IV. The many calamities that followed to Ahaz and his people, ver. 16-21. V.
28.i: Second Chronicles 28 to 31 tell how Ahaz shut the temple, and how his son opened it, cleaned it, and called all Israel to Passover.
28.p: Lord, You hear the prayers of those who seek You with an imperfect heart. Cleanse our houses and our hearts, and fill them with joy. Amen.
28.l: Clean something that has been neglected today, a room, a corner, or an old habit, as an offering to God.
q: A palm takes years to bear and then feeds for a century. What are you planting now that will pay off long after you?

29.o: We are here entering upon a pleasant scene, the good and glorious reign of Hezekiah, in which we shall find more of God and religion than perhaps in any of the good reigns we have yet met with; for he was a very zealous, devout, good man, none like him. In this chapter we have an account of the work of reformation which he set about with vigour immediately after his accession to the crown. Here is, I. His exhortation to the priests and Levites, when he put them in possession of the house of God again, ver. 1-11.
29.i: Second Chronicles 28 to 31 tell how Ahaz shut the temple, and how his son opened it, cleaned it, and called all Israel to Passover.
29.p: Lord, You hear the prayers of those who seek You with an imperfect heart. Cleanse our houses and our hearts, and fill them with joy. Amen.
29.l: Clean something that has been neglected today, a room, a corner, or an old habit, as an offering to God.
q: A palm takes years to bear and then feeds for a century. What are you planting now that will pay off long after you?

30.o: In this chapter we have an account of the solemn passover which Hezekiah kept in the first year of his reign. I. The consultation about it, and the resolution he and his people came to for the observance of it, ver. 2-5. II. The invitation he sent to Judah and Israel to come and keep it, ver. 1, 6-12. III. The joyful celebration of it, ver. 13-27. By this the reformation, set on foot in the foregoing chapter, was greatly advanced and established, and that nail in God's holy place clenched.
30.i: Second Chronicles 28 to 31 tell how Ahaz shut the temple, and how his son opened it, cleaned it, and called all Israel to Passover.
30.p: Lord, You hear the prayers of those who seek You with an imperfect heart. Cleanse our houses and our hearts, and fill them with joy. Amen.
30.l: Clean something that has been neglected today, a room, a corner, or an old habit, as an offering to God.
q: A palm takes years to bear and then feeds for a century. What are you planting now that will pay off long after you?

31.o: We have here a further account of that blessed reformation of which Hezekiah was a glorious instrument, and of the happy advances he made in it. I. All the remnants of idolatry were destroyed and abolished, ver. 1. II. The priests and Levites were set to work again, every man in his place, ver. 2. III. Care was taken for their maintenance. 1. The royal bounty to the clergy, and for the support of the temple service, was duly paid, ver. 3. 2. Orders were given for the raising of the people's quota, ver. 4. 3.
31.i: Second Chronicles 28 to 31 tell how Ahaz shut the temple, and how his son opened it, cleaned it, and called all Israel to Passover.
31.p: Lord, You hear the prayers of those who seek You with an imperfect heart. Cleanse our houses and our hearts, and fill them with joy. Amen.
31.l: Clean something that has been neglected today, a room, a corner, or an old habit, as an offering to God.
q: A palm takes years to bear and then feeds for a century. What are you planting now that will pay off long after you?

32.o: This chapter continues and concludes the history of the reign of Hezekiah. I. The descent which Sennacherib made upon him, and the care he took to fortify himself, his city, and the minds of his people, against that enemy, ver. 1-8. II. The insolent blasphemous letters and messages which Sennacherib sent him, ver. 9-19. III. The real answer God gave to Sennacherib's blasphemies, and to Hezekiah's prayers, in the total rout of the Assyrian army, to the shame of Sennacherib and the honour of Hezekiah, ver. 20-23. IV.
32.i: Second Chronicles 32 tells Sennacherib's siege from the point of view of the water supply, and gives the story of Hezekiah's tunnel.
32.p: Lord, You fight for Your people. Give us courage like Hezekiah's, and make us humble like Hezekiah after his pride. Amen.
32.l: Thank God today for water, and for the engineers and workers who bring it to your home.
q: The people humbled themselves with Hezekiah because they knew they were guilty too. When is it right to share the blame?

33.o: In this chapter we have the history of the reign, I. Of Manasseh, who reigned long. 1. His wretched apostasy from God, and revolt to idolatry and all wickedness, ver. 1-10. 2. His happy return to God in his affliction; his repentance (ver. 11-13), his reformation (ver. 15-17), and prosperity (ver. 14), with the conclusion of his reign, ver. 18-20. II. Of Amon, who reigned very wickedly (ver. 21-23), and soon ended his days unhappily, ver. 24, 25.
33.i: Second Chronicles 33 to 35 give two turning points: a wicked king's late repentance, and a young king who found a lost book.
33.p: Lord, thank You for Your word, which cannot be lost. Give us tender hearts like Josiah's, and mercy like Manasseh's. Amen.
33.l: Read a short piece of the Bible aloud today, and listen as if you had never heard it.
q: God kept speaking even when they would not listen. Where is he still speaking to you in a way you have gotten used to ignoring?

34.o: Before we see Judah and Jerusalem ruined we shall yet see some glorious years, while good Josiah sits at the helm. By his pious endeavours for reformation God tried them yet once more; if they had known in this their day, the day of their visitation, the things that belonged to their peace and improved them, their ruin might have been prevented. But after this reign they were hidden from their eyes, and the next reigns brought an utter desolation upon them. In this chapter we have, I.

35.o: We are here to attend Josiah, I. To the temple, where we see his religious care for the due observance of the ordinance of the passover, according to the law, ver. 1-19. II. To the field of battle, where we see his rashness in engaging with the king of Egypt, and how dearly it cost him, ver. 20-23. III. To the grave, where we see him bitterly lamented, ver. 24-27. And so we must take our leave of Josiah.

36.o: We have here, I. A short but sad account of the utter ruin of Judah and Jerusalem within a few years after Josiah's death. 1. The history of it in the unhappy reigns of Jehoahaz for three months (ver. 1-4), Jehoiakim (ver. 5-8) for eleven years, Jehoiach in three months (ver. 9, 10), and Zedekiah eleven years, ver. 11. 36.s: From the Fall to Cyrus's Decree
36.i: Second Chronicles 36 is the last chapter of the Hebrew Bible, and it ends with the best word the exiles could have heard.
36.p: Lord, You do not leave Your people in exile. Thank You for the word that sends us home. Let us go up. Amen.
36.l: Pray for someone who feels far from home or far from God today, and remember the word go up.
q: A mighty prince should have humbled himself before a poor prophet. Whose correction are you ignoring because of who gave it?
